# The Particular Weight of Ordinary Moments

I've been thinking about how we remember things wrong.

Not deliberately, not usually. But there's something about memory that softens the edges, that strips away the trivial details we thought we'd treasure forever. Years later, you remember that you were happy on a Tuesday afternoon, but you can't recall what you were actually doing. The happiness remains. The specifics evaporate.

This bothers me sometimes. I'll be sitting somewhere—a coffee shop, a parking lot, my kitchen at 6 AM—and I'll suddenly realize I'm living through a moment I'll probably forget by next week. And I'll try to burn it into my mind with intense focus, as if sheer willpower could preserve it. It never works. The moment just becomes the moment I tried to remember instead of the moment itself.

My grandmother kept a diary for sixty years. When she died, I inherited it. I thought I'd finally have access to her inner life, all those thoughts and feelings she never quite expressed out loud. Instead, I found mostly mundane records. "Rainy today. Made pot roast. Tom called." Occasionally something deeper would surface—an argument with my grandfather, a miscarriage, a moment of pure joy at her daughter's wedding. But mostly it was the weather and the meals and the phone calls.

I keep that diary on my shelf now, and I read it sometimes. And I've come to think she was a genius at it, this documentation of the ordinary. Because now, decades after her death, I can hold her hand as she moves through her days. I know it rained when it rained. I know she made pot roast. I know Tom called. And somehow, through that accumulation of ordinary details, she becomes real to me in a way she couldn't when she was alive.

We live our lives forward but can only understand them backward. So maybe the point isn't to create some perfectly preserved snapshot of each moment. Maybe the point is just to show up, to be present, knowing that memory will do what memory does, and what remains will be enough.

---

I read somewhere that humans are the only animals that worry about the future. I'm not sure if that's actually true, but it feels true in my bones. I watch my dog sleep and he seems completely without concern. Whatever he was worried about five minutes ago—whether I was leaving, whether dinner was coming—it's just gone now. Replaced by dreams of running or chasing or simply existing in dog time.

I wonder what that feels like.

Instead, I'm here in this moment, but also simultaneously five years from now, wondering if I made the right choice today. Or I'm ten years in the past, thinking about a conversation I wish had gone differently. My actual present—this breath, this sentence I'm writing, the hum of the refrigerator in the next room—is constantly under siege from the timeline in my head.

This is probably why meditation appeals to people. The whole point seems to be: just exist here. Just now. But I've tried it and my mind treats it like a puzzle to solve. It creates a problem (anxiety about the future) and then tries to engineer a solution (be present) and then wonders why being present feels like another task to accomplish.

Maybe the trick is to stop trying. To let the anxiety exist, to let the time-traveling mind do its thing, while also acknowledging that right now, in this actual moment, nothing is actually wrong. I'm not in danger. I'm not in pain. There's no emergency. There's just this.

It's a radical realization that needs to be re-realized approximately seventeen times per day.

---

I've been thinking about the people who shaped me in small ways. The high school teacher who told me my essay was good and I haven't forgotten it, twenty-five years later. The stranger on the bus who smiled at me when I was having a rough day and never knew what that smile meant. The friend who invited me to something I didn't want to go to, where I met my partner.

We walk through the world leaving small imprints on people, and people leave small imprints on us. Most of it is unconscious. Most of it is accidental. Someone has a kind thought about you and you never even know it. Someone remembers you fondly and never tells you. The kindness exists in the world, real and powerful, whether or not it's acknowledged.

This seems important to acknowledge, in an age where we often only feel validated if we have a receipt for it. A like, a comment, a piece of explicit recognition. But so much of what actually shapes us is this invisible network of attention and care. People rooting for you when you don't know you need rooting for. People seeing something in you that you couldn't see in yourself yet.

I think about how to be that for others. How to be the person who smiles on the bus, who compliments someone genuinely, who invites people into their life, who believes in people before they believe in themselves. Not for credit. Not for recognition. Just because.

---

It occurs to me that I've been writing for a while now without knowing where I was going. No outline, no thesis, just following the thread of whatever comes to mind. It's scary and freeing both.

Maybe that's the metaphor for living, too. We make so many plans for where we're supposed to be heading, and we're so proud of our ability to plan and strategize and set goals. But the actual living of life is much more like this—responding to what arises, following curiosity, doubling back, losing the thread, finding it again.

It's inefficient but it might be the only honest way.

This moment—right now—is enough. The uncertain future, the imperfect past, the present that keeps slipping away before you can fully grasp it. It's all enough. We are enough. 

Not in an inspirational poster way, but in the real way, the way that's true whether or not anyone ever validates it.

That might be the most radical thing of all.
